==Problem==

There is a positive integer <math>n</math> such that <math>(n+1)! + (n+2)! = n! \cdot 440</math>. What is the sum of the digits of <math>n</math>?

<math>\textbf{(A) }3\qquad\textbf{(B) }8\qquad\textbf{(C) }10\qquad\textbf{(D) }11\qquad\textbf{(E) }12</math>

==Solution==
===Solution 1===

<cmath>\begin{split}& (n+1)n! + (n+2)(n+1)n! = 440 \cdot n! \\
\Rightarrow \ &n![n+1 + (n+2)(n+1)] = 440 \cdot n! \\
\Rightarrow \ &n + 1 + n^2 + 3n + 2 = 440 \\
\Rightarrow \ &n^2 + 4n - 437 = 0\end{split}</cmath>

Solving by the quadratic formula, <imath>n = \frac{-4\pm \sqrt{16+437\cdot4}}{2} = \frac{-4\pm 42}{2} = \frac{38}{2} = 19</imath> (since clearly <imath>n \geq 0</imath>). The answer is therefore <imath>1 + 9 = \boxed{\textbf{(C) }10}</imath>.

===Solution 2===

Dividing both sides by <imath>n!</imath> gives
<cmath>(n+1)+(n+2)(n+1)=440 \Rightarrow n^2+4n-437=0 \Rightarrow (n-19)(n+23)=0.</cmath>

Instead of prime factorizing 437, which could take some time, we can notice that the two factors of 437 we need (if they exist) need to be pretty close - their difference is 4. Then, we can try a few numbers close to <imath> \sqrt{400} = 20 </imath>, so we find 19 and 23 as factors.

Since <imath>n</imath> is non-negative, <imath>n=19</imath>. The answer is <imath>1 + 9 = \boxed{\textbf{(C) }10}</imath>.

===Solution 3===

Dividing both sides by <imath>n!</imath> as before gives <imath>(n+1)+(n+1)(n+2)=440</imath>. Now factor out <imath>(n+1)</imath>, giving <imath>(n+1)(n+3)=440</imath>. By considering the prime factorization of <imath>440</imath>, a bit of experimentation gives us <imath>n+1=20</imath> and <imath>n+3=22</imath>, so <imath>n=19</imath>, so the answer is <imath>1 + 9 = \boxed{\textbf{(C) }10}</imath>.

===Solution 4===

Since <imath>(n+1)! + (n+2)! = (n+1)n! + (n+2)(n+1)n! = 440 \cdot n!</imath>, the result can be factored into <imath>(n+1)(n+3)n!=440 \cdot n!</imath> and divided by <imath>n!</imath> on both sides to get <imath>(n+1)(n+3)=440</imath>. From there, it is easier to complete the square with the quadratic <imath>(n+1)(n+3) = n^2 + 4n + 3</imath>, so <imath>n^2+4n+4=441 \Rightarrow (n+2)^2=441</imath>. Solving for <imath>n</imath> results in <imath>n=19,-23</imath>, and since <imath>n>0</imath>, <imath>n=19</imath> and the answer is <imath>1 + 9 = \boxed{\textbf{(C) }10}</imath>.

~Randomlygenerated

===Solution 5===

Rewrite <imath>(n+1)! + (n+2)! = 440 \cdot n!</imath> as <imath>(n+1)n! + (n+2)(n+1)n! = 440 \cdot n!.</imath> Factoring out the <imath>n!</imath> we get <imath>n!(n + 1 + (n+1)(n+2)) = 440 \cdot n!.</imath> Expand this to get <imath>n!(n^2 + 4n + 3) = 440 \cdot n!.</imath> Factor this and divide by <imath>n!</imath> to get <imath>(n + 1)(n + 3) = 440.</imath> If we take the prime factorization of <imath>440</imath> we see that it is <imath>2^3 * 5 * 11.</imath> Intuitively, we can find that <imath>n + 1 = 20</imath> and <imath>n + 3 = 22.</imath> Therefore, <imath>n = 19.</imath> Since the problem asks for the sum of the didgits of <imath>n</imath>, we finally calculate <imath>1 + 9 = 10</imath> and get answer choice <imath>\boxed{\textbf{(C) }10}</imath>.

~pnacham

===Solution 6===

Factor out <imath>n!</imath> from the left side of the equation:
<cmath> (n+1)! + (n+2)! = (n+1)n! + (n+2)(n+1)n! </cmath>
<cmath> = (n+1)n! \left[ 1 + (n+2) \right] </cmath>
<cmath> = (n+1)(n+3) \cdot n! </cmath>

Setting this equal to the given expression <imath>440 \cdot n!</imath>:
<cmath> (n+3)(n+1) \cdot n! = 440 \cdot n! </cmath>

Dividing both sides by <imath>n!</imath>:
<cmath> (n+3)(n+1) = 440 </cmath>

To solve for <imath>n</imath>, let <imath>a = n+2</imath>. Then <imath>(n+3) = a+1</imath> and <imath>(n+1) = a-1</imath>:
<cmath> (a+1)(a-1) = 440 </cmath>
<cmath> a^2 - 1 = 440 </cmath>
<cmath> a^2 = 441 </cmath>
<cmath> a = 21 </cmath>

Substituting back for <imath>n</imath>:
<cmath> n+2 = 21 \implies n = 19 </cmath>

The sum of the digits of <imath>n</imath> is <imath>1 + 9 = \boxed{10}</imath>.

~Ipimath

===Solution 7 (Simpler Solution 1, No Experimentation)===

Like in solution 1, continue until <imath>n^2 + 4n - 437 = 0</imath>

Quadratic formula:

<cmath>\frac{-4 \pm \sqrt{1764}}{2}</cmath>.

Because <imath>n</imath> is an integer, assume 1764 is a perfect square. The last digit of 1764 is 4, meaning that the number <imath>k^2 = 1764</imath>, <imath>k</imath> ends in either 2 or 8. Then, <imath>\sqrt{16} < \sqrt{17} < \sqrt{25}</imath>, so taking the former of the two, we have that our possible square roots are 42 or 48. It then follows that <imath>40^2 < k^2 < 50^2</imath>, and that <imath>k^2</imath> is much closer to <imath>40^2</imath> than <imath>50^2</imath>, so our desired <imath>k = 42</imath>. It follows that <imath>n = 19</imath> and the sum of the digits is <imath>\boxed{10}</imath>.

~Pinotation
